item.title: The Question AI Can’t Answer for You
item.description:
Decision-Making

The Question AI Can’t Answer for You

Knowing what we value matters more in an age of AI-assisted decisions.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • People increasingly use AI for major life decisions, making discernment a new human skill.
  • The efficiency of AI is useful, but the most meaningful choice is not always the most efficient one.
  • The usefulness of AI advice depends partly on how clearly we understand what we value in the first place.
  • AI can help us compare options, but it cannot determine what a moment should mean in the context of our lives.
An Inconvenient Trip Worth the Hassle
Source: Lindsey Godwin/ Chat GPT/ Used with permission

This past week, I flew from Cleveland to Vermont so that I could be home for about 12 hours and there for my daughter’s last first day of high school. I recently started a new position in Cleveland while my husband and daughter remain in Vermont for her senior year, which has made “being there” a little more logistically complicated than it used to be.

By any definition, the trip was not an efficient use of time. After I got to the airport, flew to Vermont, slept for a few hours, got up the next morning, took the obligatory first-day photo, hugged my daughter, and headed back to the airport, I had spent far more time traveling than I had actually spent with her. There also wasn’t anything I particularly needed to do in Vermont. This wasn’t kindergarten or college drop-off, and she could have started her senior year perfectly well without me standing on the front steps that morning. I simply wanted to be there because, somewhere in the calculus of this season of our lives, that moment mattered to me.

The experience has me reflecting on how we know which moments are worth inconveniencing ourselves for. We make these calculations all the time, asking ourselves things like: Is it worth the drive? Can I afford the flight? Do I have time? Could we celebrate another weekend?

Increasingly, we are also turning to AI to help us sort through questions like these. A 2026 Yale Youth Poll found that 21 percent of registered voters surveyed had asked AI for advice about major life decisions, including roughly a third of adults under 45 (Yale Youth Poll, 2026). Honestly, I understand the appeal. When I have a messy decision in front of me, there is real value in being able to lay out the variables and have something help me see what I might be missing.

Psychologists have long used the term cognitive offloading to describe our tendency to use tools outside ourselves to reduce the mental effort required to complete tasks. Today, AI extends that possibility into increasingly complex forms of planning, reasoning, and decision-making (Abrams, 2026).

I am happy to offload some mental work from time to time. Let AI find the better flight, compare schedules, point out an option I overlooked, or help me untangle competing demands. Given how stretched most of us already feel, that is no small thing. But my Vermont trip made me wonder where the useful offloading ends.

Had I asked AI whether I should go, I could have supplied plenty of data: my calendar, the cost of the ticket, travel time, work commitments, and the multiple airport runs I was asking of my husband. I could have added that family is important to me and that I hate missing milestones. With enough context, I suspect it could have helped me think through the decision quite thoughtfully.

article continues after advertisement

What I still had to determine for myself was the weight I gave this particular moment.

For me, part of what gave the moment its weight was the awareness that it belonged to a narrowing window of time. Laura Carstensen’s work on socioemotional selectivity theory suggests that our perception of time shapes what we prioritize. When the future feels expansive, we tend to be drawn toward exploration, information, and future possibilities. As we become more aware that time is limited, emotionally meaningful goals and relationships tend to move toward the foreground (Carstensen et al., 1999).

Ersner-Hershfield and colleagues (2008) take that idea one step further. They found that when people become aware they are experiencing something for the last time, the ending itself can intensify the experience. They describe the resulting mixture of happiness and sadness as poignancy.

A “last first day” comes conveniently labeled that way, but most of life does not. We rarely know when we are reading the last bedtime story or taking the last family vacation when everyone still lives under the same roof. We don’t know when a child will stop reaching for our hand in a parking lot, when a friendship will quietly change shape, or when an ordinary afternoon with someone we love will later become one we wish we could have back. Milestones occasionally do us the favor of making time visible.

What I keep coming back to after this 12-hour trip is that some decisions ask for more than a good calculation. They ask us to notice what is fleeting and what carries enough meaning to warrant some inconvenience.

So perhaps I need a different set of questions alongside the practical ones: Does this moment have an expiration date? What might my presence mean to someone I love? When I look back, am I more likely to remember the inconvenience or be grateful that I went? And perhaps most importantly, Is this one of my moments?

This is not a mandate to show up for everything. If every event and gathering becomes something we absolutely must attend, meaning quickly turns into obligation. The goal is to get better at discerning what matters enough to us to warrant the inconvenience.

And this is where I have come to see a useful boundary around what I ask of AI. I can ask it to help me see my options, challenge my assumptions, or even help me articulate what I value. What I cannot hand over is the responsibility for deciding how much weight those values should carry in a particular decision.

I will keep using AI to help me in certain decisions because in many cases, it helps me see options and tradeoffs more clearly. What this trip reminded me, however, is that before I can use any of that information well, I still have to know what I am trying to protect, prioritize, or make room for in my life. That part of the decision comes from somewhere more personal than calculation.

article continues after advertisement

In this case, I knew that being there mattered. AI could have helped me think through how to make the trip work, but determining that this was a moment worth making room for was still a decision only I could make.

item.title: 9 Everyday Phrase Substitutions That Can Promote Success
item.description:
Self-Help

9 Everyday Phrase Substitutions That Can Promote Success

Help yourself become stronger and more confident by changing your language.

Posted August 30, 2026

Source: Nathan Hansen Illustrations

The words we use affect how we feel and act. In this post we will review nine everyday substitutions you can use to make you stronger and more confident.

1. Instead of saying, “I’ll try” say, “I will” or “I want to”

Why?: “Try” is a negative word. When you say that you have tried something in the past, usually this means that you did not succeed. Trying leaves a lot of room for the possibility of failure, and may lead your brain down a dead-end path. On the other hand, doing something and wanting it are both positive actions.

2. Instead of saying, “I don’t have...” say, “I want” or “I wish” or “I’ll do my best to”

Why?: No matter how you use it, “don’t” is a negative. Whenever you can choose a positive phrase instead of a negative one, choose the positive one. I want to have friends so that I can… is a far more hopeful statement than I don’t have any friends. I want can be the beginning of an action plan.

3. Instead of saying, “This is dumb” or “This is annoying” say, “I can learn one thing from this” (even if it’s a what-not-to-do)

Why?: There is always something to gain or learn from every experience, even a negative, boring, or sad one. Making this small change will help you get in the habit of looking for that positive takeaway.

4. Instead of saying, “This is my fault” or “This is your fault” say “Let’s think about what happened” or “Let’s talk about what we do next” or “How can I make this better?”

Why?: Assigning blame as a punitive statement is negative and it’s all about the past. When you’re focused on the future, you can also focus on resolving problems instead of dragging them out. Understanding what happened is important, but dwelling on blame often keeps us stuck. Once responsibility is understood, asking "What can we do next?" moves us toward solutions.

5. Instead of saying, “You are..." say “What you could do better is..."

Why?: When you label a person pejoratively, that’s a personal attack, one that can be hurtful and can cause that person to fight back or shut down. When you suggest a solution, you leave room for negotiation and change.

6. Instead of saying, “Why me?” say “What next?”

Why?: Every life has hardship, sometimes more than seems fair. But the one thing you can always control is what you are going to do about your troubles.

7. Instead of saying, “Sorry to bother you” say, “May I have a few minutes of your time?”

Why?: There is no reason to apologize for existing, for having a need, for asking a question, or for taking up a little bit of someone’s time. Approach people with politeness and confidence.

article continues after advertisement

8. Instead of saying, “I hate doing..." say, "I'm going to feel good when this is done" or "I can get through this."

Why?: Using negative words to talk about a task you don’t enjoy has a way of making it even more unpleasant. When you frame your intentions in terms of feeling better and getting it done, you’ll find it easier to finish.

9. Instead of saying, “If...” say, “When...” and “How…”

Why?: Speaking about “if” things happen implies they may not work out. This can sow doubt in your mind and make you less likely to succeed. Speaking about things you want to happen and how they will happen as if they are a future reality is a way of asking your subconscious to help make them happen.

Takeaway

When you make intentional shifts in the words you choose, you can shift your mind from doubt and blame toward confidence, resilience, and action.

This post post is excerpted from my book, The Life Guide for Teens.

item.title: What We Get Wrong About Internalized Homophobia
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

What We Get Wrong About Internalized Homophobia

Deshaming a common defense mechanism among gay men.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Research has linked internalized homophobia with greater psychological distress among sexual minority men.
  • Internalized homophobia can affect gay men even when they consciously reject homophobic beliefs.
  • Like skin, our defenses protect us until we eventually outgrow them.
Source: Jed Villejo / Unsplash

When I was beginning my training to become a therapist, I asked a mentor of mine why he became a therapist.

In his beautiful, sanctuary-like office in the heart of West Hollywood, he looked at me and pointed out the window toward the Pacific Design Center, near the epicenter of gay bars, and said, "Because out there is bullshit, in here is the truth.”

I knew exactly what he meant because I had spent years living the BS myself.

For 11 years, I worked at one of the busiest and most popular gay bars in West Hollywood. It wasn't uncommon to see high-powered Hollywood professionals—including agents of some of the most well-known celebrities—partying late into the night, making out with men, and then returning to lives where being gay was compartmentalized enough it never crossed over into their public or professional identities.

Less than five minutes away, just down the street, was the national headquarters of The Trevor Project—a suicide prevention and crisis intervention organization for LGBTQ youth. It is an entire organization dedicated to supporting young people who feel like they can't be themselves—who've been taught, explicitly or implicitly, that who they are is somehow too much, or not enough.

Many of my friends talked to me in private about their struggles while living very different lives out in West Hollywood or on social media. I became a therapist because I had navigated the same challenges myself, and I wanted to offer gay men something I hadn't always had access to: a clinician who understood the unique experiences of growing up gay in a world that either ignored, distorted, or devalued who we are.

As part of my specialization in LGBTQ Affirmative Psychology, I learned how to provide affirming mental health care for LGBTQ individuals while also applying psychological theory to issues impacting gender and sexual minorities.

Much of my clinical work at the Los Angeles LGBT Center involved helping clients recognize and challenge the shameful messages they'd internalized about being gay. While most of my clients could consciously recognize that the anti-LGBTQ messages they'd heard growing up were misguided, many weren't aware of the extent to which they had unconsciously internalized external homophobia.

article continues after advertisement

What Is Internalized Homophobia?

Internalized homophobia is one of the most common experiences among gay men, yet it’s often misunderstood and remains one of the least openly talked about or acknowledged.

Internalized homophobia occurs when a gay person absorbs the negative attitudes and beliefs about being gay that he grew up around from family, religion, culture, and peers, consciously and unconsciously, and turns them inward.

At its core, internalized homophobia operates as a defense mechanism. As a defense against rejection, we learn to suppress or isolate the parts of ourselves we fear could threaten our connection to the people and communities we depend on for love, care, and support.

Internalized homophobia can also impact how we relate to other gay men, including our friendships, romantic relationships, sex lives, communities, and coping strategies. It’s subtle and persistent, making even an outwardly confident man feel like he's somehow still not enough.

What Internalized Homophobia Looks Like

You may recognize yourself in some of these statements and not others. Some may have been true for you in the past but no longer feel true today.

  • Modifying how we act depending on who we're around.
  • Feeling more comfortable when people don't know we're gay.
  • Comparing ourselves to other gay men and feeling like we don't measure up.
  • Feeling pressure to prove that we're different, or not like, other gay men.
  • Disliking or judging in other gay men what we have difficulty accepting in ourselves.
  • Having difficulty being fully open or affectionate with another man.
  • Using drugs or alcohol to have sex or connect with men.
  • Having a persistent feeling that we're not enough, no matter our accomplishments or outward markers of success.
  • Experiencing anxiety, depression, or other mental health challenges.
  • Feeling shame after sex or masturbation, judging our sexual desires, feeling uncomfortable receiving pleasure, or struggling to separate sexual desire from shame.
article continues after advertisement

Facing internalized homophobia can feel like a betrayal of the community, as if by acknowledging it, we're giving credence to the very homophobia we've fought to survive. But left unexamined, internalized homophobia is closely linked to poor mental health outcomes, higher rates of substance abuse, low self-esteem, and intimate partner violence among gay and bisexual men.

Pay attention to the statements that feel familiar, the ones you want to dismiss, and the ones that make you uncomfortable. Sometimes the reaction itself is worth looking at more closely.

Once we recognize a pattern, we have the opportunity to bring awareness to the choices we make and begin choosing what to externalize, heal, and let go.

Identifying patterns is about understanding them, not blaming ourselves.

What I've learned from my own life is that nothing is ever brought into my awareness that I'm not ready to either change or help change.

If anything came up for you that you’d like to explore more, support is available, whether through a therapist, a trusted person, or community resources like the Trevor Project or PFLAG.

item.title: How Bystanders Can De-Escalate Workplace Aggression
item.description:
Bystander Effect

How Bystanders Can De-Escalate Workplace Aggression

Coworkers are not cops, but they can help prevent violence before it occurs.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Behavioral improvement depends on whether intervention is in the moment or after the fact.
  • Successful de-escalation depends on whether the perpetrator cares about proper behavior.
  • Power dynamics impact how aggressors respond to intervention.
Source: Dimitar Veselinov / Pixabay

Unfortunately, workplace violence has become a household term in recent years, as laws evolve to keep pace with publicized incidents of violence and mass shootings. Yet within individual workplace settings, when tempers run hot, there are effective methods of cooling things down, especially when initiated by respectful peers and colleagues. Research explains.

The Buffer of Bystanders

Many people admit that when they are upset, the best candidates to calm them down are trusted family and friends. But because someone who becomes irate in the workplace is unlikely to have immediate access to their intimate circle of influence, trusted colleagues and peers may be the next best option, depending on who they are.

Ivana Vranjes et al. (2025) examined the impact of bystander intervention on interpersonal workplace aggression.[i]They recognized that the effectiveness of such intervention depends on the aggressor’s response, which will likely reflect his or her relationship with the bystander.

Vranjes et al. proposed that organizations should train bystanders to consider several factors when intervening to address a hostile employee: (1) the extent of the perpetrator’s commitment to behavior—for instance, whether or not it is intentional; (2) the timing and manner of intervention—for example, do they intervene in the moment or discuss it after the fact?; (3) whether the perpetrator is a person who cares about being moral and behaving as expected; and (4) the relationship and relative power the bystander has as compared with the perpetrator—which will likely impact how the perpetrator will respond to the intervention.

Power Dynamics and Saving Face

Vranjes et al. report that constructive bystander interventions that reduce a perpetrator's identity threat and maintain his or her sense of moral and relational identity are more likely to be effective. They suggest that these interventions decrease the risk of retaliation and are particularly useful when the bystander has less power than the aggressor. They describe one benefit of constructive interventions being that they consider the perspective of the perpetrator, affording them the opportunity to rethink and reconstruct their behavior going forward, reducing the potential for future aggression.

Vranjes et al. note that constructive interventions are appropriate only when aggression has not caused severe harm to a victim. In cases of severe aggression with substantial damage to a victim, such as occurs in cases of bullying, formal action might be necessary. This type of action requires the bystander to be more powerful than the aggressor to protect their safety, as well as the victim. They caution, however, about potential covert aggression that may continue even after intervention from a powerful bystander.

article continues after advertisement

Intervention Requires Management Involvement

As with any policy, effective workplace strategy requires clear rules and regulations, as well as ongoing employee management and oversight. Vranjes et al. note that the success of a seemingly effective intervention will become clearer over time only when perpetrator behavior is carefully monitored, and others continue to reinforce the sentiment that aggressive behavior is unacceptable. Although peer influence can help shape employee behavior, they remind us that high-power individuals within an organization have a responsibility to address workplace aggression and should promote top-down approaches to this issue instead of delegating behavioral management solely to employees' own efforts.

Aggressors Respond Differently

Vranjes et al. conclude that although bystander intervention can be a powerful method of potentially reducing interpersonal workplace aggression, it can be ineffective and even potentially harmful when an aggressor perceives identity threat and reacts defensively. They acknowledge that although defensiveness may be expected, some perpetrators are able to react more productively, viewing the intervention as an opportunity for growth. They also note that different individuals experience threats to moral and relational identity differently and respond accordingly due to a personal process of sensemaking. Some aggressors react punitively by escalating hostility, while others adopt a more restorative approach such as apologizing to the victim of their animosity. Vranjes et al. also note that the reactions of others, as well as the passage of time, can prompt further sensemaking, altering an aggressor’s initial reaction to an incident.

Bystanders can make a positive difference on the behavior of workplace aggressors and should proactively think through how they would address peers and colleagues within a situation creating animosity—before it occurs.

item.title: Patient Privacy on Healthcare Websites
item.description:
Law and Crime

Patient Privacy on Healthcare Websites

How to protect personal information shared through providers’ online platforms.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Psychologists have ethical duties to maintain client privacy, including with online platforms.
  • Online mental health platforms may provide convenience and clinical benefits.
  • Online platforms can also create privacy and security risks.
  • Before sharing information, patients should ask how it will be collected, protected, and disclosed.

When patients share personal information with healthcare or mental healthcare providers, those providers have ethical duties to maintain the privacy and confidentiality of the information they collect (ACA, 2014; AMA, n.d.;. APA, 2017; NASW, 2021). Professionals covered by the Health Insurance Portability and Protection Act (HIPAA, 1996) also have legal duties to safeguard personal health information. Privacy and confidentiality may be particularly important for patients concerned about mental health stigma, embarrassment, workplace discrimination, or other potential consequences of disclosure.

A recent case, Santoro v. Tower Health, illustrates the privacy concerns that can arise when patients communicate with providers through websites. A group of patients alleged that a healthcare system’s use of Meta Pixel—a tracking technology—shared identifiable health with Meta, a large social media company, for advertising and other commercial purposes. The patients claimed that these practices violated their privacy rights.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for Third Circuit ultimately dismissed the case, finding that the pleadings were not sufficiently specific. While the court did not actually decide whether the sharing of information violated patient privacy laws, the case does raise interesting issues for patients who are asked to share personal information on their providers’ websites.

This post explores related issues from the perspective of mental health patients who receive requests from their psychologist to submit information electronically as part of their assessment or treatment processes.

Rationale for Requesting Online Submission of Patient Information

Psychologists may have various reasons for asking patients to submit information online. For example, they use electronic forms to gather intake information, to screen for emergency situations, to assess a patient’s concerns, or guide the psychologist’s next steps with the patient. For both patients and psychologists, online submission may enhance the efficiency of the process, helping the psychologist to be better prepared for future discussions and treatment options.

Some mental health websites also provide patients with information, exercises, and other resources that may help them understand and manage their concerns more effectively. For instance, a psychologist might use online interventions to guide patients through problem-solving processes, exercises to build empathy or self-esteem, mood monitoring, or mindfulness practices.

These technologies can make services more convenient and accessible. Convenience, however, should not come at the expense of privacy, patient choice, or clinical effectiveness.

Informed Consent

If a psychologist asks you to submit information electronically, you have a right to understand why the information is being requested, as well as how it will be used. Psychologists and other mental health professionals all have duties to provide clients with an opportunity for fully informed consent (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; NASW, 2021).

article continues after advertisement

Before submitting information, consider asking:

  • What information is being collected?
  • Why do you need this information?
  • Who will have access to the information?
  • Will the information become part of my clinical record?
  • How long will the information be stored and how will it be deleted?
  • Could the information be shared for research, advertising, product development, or other purposes?
  • What are the potential risks for my privacy and the security of this information?

If you do not wish to submit information online, ask your psychologist for other options (e.g., paper forms; meeting in person or on videoconference for an intake or assessment interview; referral to another provider). While an alternative may not always be available, your psychologist should explain whether using technology is required and what declining it would mean for your services.

Confidentiality

As noted earlier, psychologists have duties to protect your privacy and confidentiality. If you have questions about how information that you share online will be protected, ask.

Your psychologist should be able to tell you whether the technology they are using is HIPAA-compliant, the legal standard for protection of personal health information by healthcare providers. You may also ask whether the information will be shared with others, under what circumstances, and for what purposes.

It is important to ask whether the website uses cookies, pixels, analytics tools, or other tracking technologies. These tools may collect information about the pages you visit, the links you select, your location, your device, or the health concerns you research. These types of data might risk revealing personal information that may want kept private.

article continues after advertisement

You have a right to refuse to use particular websites or technology, including the avoidance of situations in which your information may be sold to other companies for research or commercial purposes. Sometimes, nonidentifying information may be shared – for instance, information about your mental health condition and treatment history, but not your name, address, or other personally identifying information. You might agree to such uses, knowing that the information may be helpful to others without putting you at significant risk. Still, there may be some risk that this information could be reconnected with you.

Conclusion

With psychologists and other mental health professionals increasing their use of AI, online intake and assessment forms, patient portals, intervention apps, and other technology to facilitate information gathering and treatment processes, it is important for patients to understand their rights to privacy, confidentiality, and informed consent. When in doubt, ask questions before you share information electronically. Find out how secure the technology is. Verify whether the technology is HIPAA-compliant: “Do you have a Business Associates Agreement with the provider to ensure the privacy of my information?” Also, consider the relative effectiveness of the technology compared with in-person services or other options.

Knowledge is power. In the context of online mental health services, knowledge also helps protect your dignity, autonomy, respect, trust, and safety.

item.title: The Danger Stalkers Still Pose
item.description:
Stalking

The Danger Stalkers Still Pose

What we know about threats posed by persistent stalkers.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • A disturbing case has brought stalking behavior back into the media.
  • The percentage of people affected by stalkers has increased and technology has enabled their surveillance.
  • Our ability to predict a specific potential threat to a stalking victim still falls short.

In Wisconsin recently, investigators discovered human skulls and items related to serial killers in the home of a man who’s been stalking a former girlfriend in Wisconsin for 13 years. Benjamin Larson, 47, was charged with a felony count of stalking. He claims his therapist gave him some tips. If so, it’s likely the therapist didn’t know everything the cops discovered.

Larson had briefly dated his victim in 2013, but things got intense. He apparently revealed his obsession with serial killer Ed Gein. When he threatened to end his life, she broke everything off and left the area. He pursued her with emails and gifts. He entered therapy, and the therapist allegedly reached out to the woman. She ignored all attempts to contact her. Larson claims his therapist told him she’d have to respond if he filed a complaint. (It’s unclear if this allegation is true.) He showed her he’d kept tabs on her, including an awareness of her marriage and new address.

But there was more.

In Larson’s home on August 14, investigators from the Sheriff’s Office found a rubbing from Ed Gein’s gravestone, 10 binders labeled “Edward Gein Book,” and a label on a jar that supposedly contained part of John Wayne Gacy's brain. On shelves were human skulls. A padlocked room revealed a sex doll and a painting of a nude that resembled the victim, along with framed images of her. Larson apparently had items that belonged to her, including an earring and images of things she’d written. Books in his home referenced the psychology of stalking. In one piece of writing, Larson stated that he’d visited the woman’s home with a machete and stole bags of her trash. He reportedly expressed his frustration over her marriage and child, writing, “It’s at [a] time like this where I really ache to take their skulls, all of them.”

He was released on bond.

I recalled from my past research on stalkers that not all who seemed threatening were lethal. In fact, most weren't. But some had been quite intent on harm. I decided to look up more recent stats. It turns out, things haven't gotten much better.

Stalking Statistics, Then and Now

In 2008, the DOJ's Bureau of Justice stated that during a 12-month period from 2005-2006, an estimated 3.4 million Americans were stalked. More than one-third were followed or monitored, and over 75% knew their stalker, usually from a romantic association. Most victims were between 18 and 24, and many had to leave a job to elude the unwanted attention. It was estimated then that at least one in 12 women had been stalked, and one out of every 45 men. One in four stalkers who'd threatened harm had carried it out—including damage to property or injury to pets. The targeted people most likely to be murdered (though rare) had been in a relationship with their stalkers.

What do we know now?

In 2019, the DOJ retained similar numbers of 1.3% (3.4 million) of persons age 16 or older being victims of stalking, a decline from 1.5% three years earlier. Females were stalked more than twice as often as males. Cyberstalking had risen.

In 2026, The National Center for Victims of Crime showed a different picture. They count 13.5 million targets, with nearly one in three women and one in six men experiencing stalking, and more than half of victims reporting this before age 25. There was an increased use by stalkers of surveillance technology. Nearly three-quarters of victims had been threatened with harm and 84% were fearful of it (up from 67% in 2019). Eight out of ten stalkers were acquaintances or former romantic partners. One in seven stalking victims relocated.

article continues after advertisement

The most prevalent form of stalking is surveillance and standing outside the victim’s home or workplace (77%), unwanted calls (52%), unwanted letters/emails (30%), and property vandalism (29.5%). Seventy to eighty percent of stalkers are male, depending on the study. About 25-40% assault their victims in some manner but are rarely deadly.

To better assess who might be dangerous, psychologist Reid Meloy offers a typology: simple obsessional (62-65%), love obsessional (25-35%), and erotomanic (3-5%). The first group, growing out of a prior relationship, is most likely to commit violence. (One study put this group at 55%.) The second type is rooted in fantasy and hope, often never having met their target. The third set hold delusional beliefs about an existing relationship with an idealized victim, usually of higher status. It’s rare and also full of bizarre notions. It’s more prevalent among females than males.

Larson’s alleged fixation seems to fall into the first category. However, the actual potential for danger in this category is pretty vague. It’s unclear whether a risk evaluation was performed before he was released, but the discoveries in his house support exercising some caution. An obsession with serial killers doesn't predict future violence, but a threat against a specific target with the means to carry it is on the list.

Despite laws enacted in every state, things have not improved much in the protection potential stalking victims. If convicted, Larson faces up to three years and six months in prison and a fine of up to $10,000. That’s probably not much comfort to his victim.

Stalking is an intrusive crime, with a heavy negative psychological impact. If the stalker uses a variety of methods for contact (or contacts the victim’s associates), the resulting stress is greater, due to the unpredictability of what might happen next. Ideally, there would be clear guidelines for how to manage an alleged long-term stalker who’s not detained. Unfortunately, the multiple shifting factors involved in future threat evaluation make this difficult. It’s likely that legal decision-makers stick to traditional practices and the victims must fend for themselves.

item.title: The Science of the Silence
item.description:
Beauty

The Science of the Silence

How community music rewires us for connection.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Live music transforms a room of strangers into an empathetic, unified community.
  • Shared anticipation in silence can synchronize heart rates and brain activity in audiences.
  • Tuning an orchestra shifts individual focus into collective neurological alignment.

With gratitude to the Loudoun Symphony Orchestra, for majestic music, community building, and for inviting our hearts and minds into the music.

As we sit in a concert hall, an auditorium, or even a church moments before the music begins, we participate in one of the most sophisticated psychological transitions known to humanity.

Before the stage lights fully swell, the air is a chaotic tapestry of sound. A flute runs rapid arpeggios in the corner; a double bass thrums a low, solitary heartbeat; a violinist expertly polishes a difficult passage. Each musician is locked in their own private bubble of performance anxiety and preparation. They are a collection of highly skilled "I's."

Then, a single oboe plays a clear, piercing A.

The Tuning A: From "I" to "We"

Woodwind Section
Source: Ashley Brody/Loudoun Symphony Orchestra, used with permission

That solitary note is a neurological summons.

As the oboe’s A reverberates through the hall, the wash of individual practice begins to form a whole. The transition is palpable. Musicians tilt their heads, actively listening outward.

  • The Section: First, they align with their immediate neighbors.
  • The Ensemble: Then, the sound sweeps across the entire stage, requiring every player to tune not just to their section, but to the entire collective.

This is a profound shift in cognitive framing. The moment individual ego surrenders to systemic coherence. The musicians are preparing to breathe with each other.

The Invisible Hours and the Swell of Connection

From the quiet sanctuary of our seats, we watch these individual players. It is impossible not to wonder about the unseen gravity behind their grace: the grueling, solitary hours spent in practice rooms and living rooms, the gentle corrections of a teacher, the late-night trials with a trusted colleague, and the endless repetition required to coax a stubborn passage into fluid art.

As the performance begins, a beautiful psychological alchemy occurs. The music swells, and with it, the individual musician rises. They transcend:

  • The Solo Musician (focused on the notes).

  • The Living History (connected to the stories of the piece).

  • The Shared Ensemble (playing with and entirely for one another).

  • The Unified Room (the fourth wall dissolves; art reaches the audience).

article continues after advertisement

The breaking of the "fourth wall" where music is no longer trapped behind an invisible barrier on the stage. Carried by the maestro’s passionate encouragement, which itself is the result of countless hours of orchestration, scheduling, and intense group rehearsal, the sound leaps from the stage to connect with the audience.

The great orchestras play to and for us. They touch us. They invite us to hear the story, to appreciate the fleeting privilege of being physically present, and to feel the sheer, physical majesty of sound vibrating in our chests. We watch these players and feel a sudden, surge of admiration, bordering on love. For their raw talent, their fierce dedication, and their willingness to let their vulnerability reach our very souls.

Karen Knobloch, Loudoun Symphony executive director, shared with us: “I have seen leading orchestras in cities such as Cleveland, NYC and others. They start the same but sometimes you are surprised and engaged in ways that are unique. Apollo’s Fire, a baroque orchestra follows the protocol but then the concertmaster begins and in this ensemble, the concertmaster plays a role that is muse, artistic leader, cheerleader, and personality galore. I literally felt the audience sort of gasp in surprise but then settle in together for the ride.”

The Ritual of Focus

We watch this unfolding ritual from the audience in quiet respect. The stage is set for a sequence of social scaffolding that guides our collective attention:

  • The Concertmaster Steps on Stage

The concertmaster (the first violinist) takes the stage to focus these disparate notes into a single, cohesive unit. Under their direction, the final adjustments are made. The tuning move from individual practice shared agreement.

  • The Maestro Enters

As the maestro walks out, a secondary wave of synchronization occurs. This time bridging the divide between the stage and the audience. The room erupts into applause. This applause, as a polite tradition, is so much more. It’s an active release of anticipation and a physical expression of appreciation for what is about to be co-created.

article continues after advertisement
  • The Great Silence Descends

Then, the maestro turns. Steps onto the podium.

Suddenly, the room undergoes a breathtaking transformation. There is no need for an usher to whisper "shush," and no neighbor needs to nudge another. A profound, heavy silence blankets the hall.

We hear the silence.

The Neuroscience of Anticipation

Stephan Matthie, Assistant Concertmaster
Source: Ashley Brody/Loudoun Symphony Orchestra, used with permission

What is happening in our brains during this moment of quiet?

From a neurobiological perspective, silence is the presence of intense neural preparation. When the maestro raises the baton, the entire room, musicians and audience, enters a state of predictive entrainment.

Our brains are highly sophisticated prediction engines. In this silence, our motor cortices prime themselves, our dopamine pathways light up with anticipation, and our autonomic nervous systems begin to mirror one another. Our breathing slows, our heart rates drop into a shared baseline, and our collective attention is corralled into a single laser-focused beam.

We are preparing to move, feel, and react as one.

The Ecology of "We": A Purpose-Driven Model

How does this miracle actually happen? It is tempting to credit only the genius of the composer or the virtuosity of the soloist. The reality is far more beautiful, sprawling, and systemic.

This moment is held together by an invisible ecosystem of shared purpose:

article continues after advertisement
  • The Performers and Maestro: Channeling years of rigorous training and collaborative hours into a single, cohesive interpretive voice.
  • The Stage and Technical Crew: The sound technicians balancing the acoustics, the lighting designers casting the perfect emotional glow, and the stagehands operating the heavy curtains with practiced, silent precision.
  • The Front of House: The ticket taker who greeted you with a smile, the usher who guided you through the dimly lit aisles, and the marketing team whose storytelling compelled you to purchase a ticket weeks ago.

Every single person, from the podium to the lobby doors, is a critical gear in this magnificent empathy machine. It is a glorious, real-world model of a purpose-driven "we." Each individual, performing their distinct role with care, contributes to a larger container designed for nothing less than collective human transcendence.

The baton drops, the music begins. Together, we are made whole.

Loudoun Symphony Orchestra.
Source: Ashley Brody/Loudoun Symphony Orchestra, used with permission

item.title: The Hidden Blessings of Romantic Breakups
item.description:
Relationships

The Hidden Blessings of Romantic Breakups

Five advantages to being unlucky in love.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • A breakup can teach you a lot about the kind of relationship you want and what you don't want.
  • You may discover that timing can be a major factor in a relationship not working.
  • Taking responsibility for your part in the breakup can lead to positive changes.
Source: Srdjan Randjelovic/Shutterstock

It can feel like a disaster. Devastating. The ultimate heartbreak. The worst thing ever to happen to you. But there may be hidden blessings to a failed relationship that become apparent over time.

With time and perspective, you may realize that there can be an upside to not living happily ever after with a partner you loved, then lost.

  1. You learn about what kind of relationship you want—and what you don’t want. Perhaps you had an attraction to bad boys—men who didn’t conform to what your parents wanted for you, men who were confirmed underachievers, men whose controlling nature you might have once believed was love. Perhaps you gravitated to physically beautiful women, regardless of their character or behavior. One patient described his ex-wife as “gorgeous on the outside but monstrous inside. Three years with her convinced me that I need a partner—a true partner—whose beauty comes from within and who is kind and compassionate."

    Another client I'll call Pam married her high school sweetheart a week after graduation and then endured twenty years of increasing misery as the man she had thought was so handsome and innately cool turned out to be abusive, entitled and addicted to alcohol and drugs. "I was so young when we married," she told me. "I didn't know life could be any different. I was in denial a lot until we had kids and I realized I didn't want my kids growing up in the chaos of our life together. Now we're divorced and I've met a man who is his total opposite: kind, considerate, an excellent communicator and a hard-working, sober person. I'm taking things slowly in this new relationship but it feels so good and so right."

  2. You realize that a particular relationship wasn’t right for you at a particular time. The right relationship at the wrong time? Perhaps. It may be that the ex-love who dreamed of home and family was not a good fit for you when you were younger and busy career-building. Your breakup may have been due to a matter of timing and clashing priorities rather than true incompatibility.

    “I dated some wonderful women when I was in college, medical school and in my internship,” my friend Mike remembers. “But at that time, I was totally focused on my career goals and, frankly, wasn't a good partner. Once established, however, I married a woman who shares many of the fine qualities of the lost loves of my past—though I think she's extra special. In our 20 years together, we've built a wonderful family. I've never been happier. There are many elements to our successful relationship but timing was definitely a factor... She came along when I was finally ready to settle down.”

  3. You gain insight into realities previously masked by fantasies and infatuation. Perhaps you were besotted with an ex-partner, imagining a glorious future together, then in total anguish when the relationship ended. But later on, you may celebrate the fact this one got away. Maybe the prince of your dreams wasn't really a very nice person. You may discover this as you reflect on the past and red flags missed or with new insights.

    “I blamed myself endlessly—and so did my mother who was disgusted that I couldn’t make the relationship with my ex-boyfriend work, even after he cheated,” a patient I’ll call Audrey told me. “I was ready to forgive and forget once again, but he broke up with me. I cried for weeks, months. Then, some years later, I ran into him and the woman he married at a social event. It was a revelation. He wasn’t a nice person. He was so arrogant and dismissive of her. I couldn’t help thinking that could have been me and I was so relieved that we broke up when we did! I had already decided that he was, in reality, Mr. Wrong. But this chance encounter validated my gratitude that we didn't end up together."

  4. You find that taking responsibility for your part in the romantic debacle gives you clues about ways you need and want to change. In the wake of a painful breakup, it’s tempting to blame the other person. A neighbor of mine, with a painful string of romantic disasters spanning decades, attributes her misfortune in love to “impossibly narcissistic men.”

    A reasonable question might be “Why do you keep falling for the same person?”

    Another even more reasonable question: “How did you contribute to this relationship not working?”

    If you want to break a pattern of pain, self-examination is crucial. The only person you can change is yourself – and you might want to challenge your own partner preferences or your behavior that seems to be problematic in relationships. It can be painful to look at your own contributions to romantic failure – but it can be a first step toward positive change.

  5. Every life experience can teach valuable lessons about who you are, what you want and how you can grow past heartbreak to love again. So rather than viewing a romantic breakup simply as a painful event to try to forget as soon as possible, reframe it as a learning experience. Think about your most recent relationship and all that it brought you: the happiness shared and the anguish of your breakup. And in both experiences, the good times and bad, what did you learn about yourself? Perhaps you’re wiser now about what it might take to grow and sustain a lasting love. You may have new inclinations to let go of romantic fantasies and to embrace what feels right for you. You may find that, beyond the pain, there are new insights and possibilities that might never have happened if not for this failed relationship.
